en: The Dharma Gate of the Samādhi of Non-contention Among All Dharmas, Volume One, composed by the Great Meditation Master Cien Nanyue Huisi. As explained in the section on the myriad practices:
from the first generation of the mind of awakening until the attainment of the Buddha-way, [one maintains] a single body and a single mind.
First is wisdom.
Because one desires to transform and teach sentient beings,
the names and designations of the myriad practices differ.
Now, one who wishes to study all the Buddha-dharmas should first maintain pure precepts and diligently practice meditative concentration,
thereby attaining all the Buddha-dharmas and the various gates of samādhi.
The one hundred and eight samādhis,
the five hundred dhāraṇīs,
and all the liberations.
Great kindness and great compassion;
the knowledge of all modes;
the five eyes.
The six supernormal powers,
the three types of clear knowledge,
and the eight liberations.
The ten powers,
the four fearlessnesses,
and the eighteen unique qualities.
The thirty-two marks,
the eighty minor characteristics,
and the six pāramitās.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,
the four great vows,
and the four immeasurable minds.
The supernormal power of fulfilling wishes,
the four means of integration,
and such immeasurable merits of the Buddha-dharma.
All arise from dhyāna. Why is this?
Because throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions, there are immeasurable Buddhas.
When one wishes to preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings,
one first enters meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) by means of the ten powers and the knowledge of the modes of the path (mārgajñatā).
He observes the differences in the faculties and natures of sentient beings,
knowing their respective remedies and the causes and conditions for attaining the Way.
Having completed his observation with the Dharma-eye,
he teaches the Dharma with the knowledge of all modes to deliver sentient beings.
The knowledge of all modes is called the Buddha-eye;
it is also called the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies.
It is also called the Samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of the Form Body (*sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi*).
Above, it manifests the bodies of all Buddhas and the bodies of all Bodhisattvas.
The body of a pratyekabuddha,
the body of an arhat,
and the bodies of various heavenly kings.
The bodies of universal wheel-turning monarchs and various minor kings;
down to the bodies of sentient beings in the three miserable realms and the six destinies—
such as all these Buddha-bodies.
The bodies of all sentient beings act simultaneously within a single thought-moment;
there is neither before nor after.
Nor is there any interval;
they preach the Dharma all at once to deliver sentient beings,
all of which is accomplished through the merit of the dhyāna-pāramitā.
Therefore, the Buddha said:
"If one does not practice seated meditation,
one will fall headlong upon level ground."
If one wishes to sever the afflictions,
first move them with meditative concentration,
and then extract them with wisdom.
Concentration is called śamatha;
wisdom is called vipaśyanā.
There are immeasurable types of concentration.
In general, three types are taught:
the lower concentration is called the concentration of the desire realm;
the middle concentration is called the concentration of the form realm.
The higher concentration is called the formless realm concentration (*ārūpya-samādhi*).
Furthermore, the lower concentration is the śrāvaka concentration,
which encompasses all three realms.
The middle concentration is the concentration of the pratyekabuddhas;
the superior concentration is the concentration of the Tathāgatas and all bodhisattvas.
Wisdom is immeasurable, yet it is said to be threefold:
first, the knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*);
second, the knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*).
Third is the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
Wisdom also has three types:
first, the wisdom of the path (mārgajñatā).
Second is the knowledge of the aspects of the path;
third is the knowledge of all aspects.
Furthermore, when analyzed in detail, there are eleven types of knowledge.
What are they? They are the knowledge of phenomena (dharma-jñāna) and conventional knowledge (saṃvṛti-jñāna).
The knowledge of others' minds,
the knowledge of past lives,
and the knowledge of suffering.
Knowledge of origination,
knowledge of cessation,
and knowledge of the path.
The knowledge of exhaustion,
the knowledge of non-arising,
and the knowledge of things as they truly are.
Furthermore, when the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*) and the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpādajñāna*) are analyzed, there are eighteen kinds of knowledge. Of these,
the knowledge of exhaustion consists of nine types.
The knowledge of non-arising consists of nine types;
these are called the eighteen knowledges. They may also be termed the eighteen minds.
The noble ones of the three vehicles all abide together within the various wisdoms of the four dhyānas.
Regarding those who inquire about the knowledge of reality as it is (yathābhūta-jñāna) on the path of reality as it is:
concerning the general and specific characteristics of all phenomena—
Because it is able to know things as they truly are,
it is called "knowledge as-it-is" (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). This refers to all such wisdoms.
This is omniscience;
it is also called non-knowledge. Why is this?
As it is said in the sūtra concerning the question posed by the brahmin Śreṇika:
the brahmin Śreṇika addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Bhagavān,
from where does the Tathāgata’s all-encompassing wisdom arise?"
The Buddha replied to Śreṇika,
"There is no place where [the Tathāgata] is found.
Śreṇika asked again:
"How is it that wisdom has no place of attainment? The Buddha answered again:
"This wisdom is not attained through internal contemplation;
this wisdom is not attained through external contemplation."
This wisdom is not attained through internal or external contemplation,
nor is it attained through non-contemplation; therefore,
there is no place where this wisdom is attained.
Therefore, it is called "ignorance," as explained in the "Chapter on the Extraordinary.
A single syllable enters into forty-two syllables.
The forty-two letters revert into a single letter,
yet even that single letter is not perceived;
only Buddhas and Buddhas thoroughly understand the nature of these letters.
One skillfully knows the dharma that is without words;
for the sake of the wordless dharma, one speaks of the dharma of words,
but not for the sake of the dharma of words does one speak of the dharma of words.
Therefore, these forty-two letters are themselves "no-letters.
Furthermore, when one wishes to practice seated meditation:
One should first contemplate the fundamental nature of the body;
this fundamental nature of the body is the *tathāgatagarbha*,
which is also termed the intrinsically pure mind (*svabhāva-viśuddha-citta*).
This is called the true mind;
it is neither within nor without.
It does not abide in the middle;
it is neither annihilated nor eternal,
nor is it even the Middle Way.
It has no name and no character;
it has no appearance;
it is neither self nor other.
Without arising and without ceasing;
without coming and without going;
without a place of abiding.
Neither delusion nor wisdom;
neither bondage nor liberation;
neither birth-and-death nor nirvana.
There is no one, two,
or many; there is no before, no after,
and no middle.
From antiquity, it has been without name or designation.
Thus concludes the contemplation of the True Body;
next, one contemplates the body of the body.
Furthermore, one contemplates the mind and body.
As for the body, it arises from the mind of deluded thought;
it undergoes retribution in accordance with karma.
In the various realms of existence, including those of devas and humans,
there is in truth no coming or going;
it is only through deluded vision that birth and extinction are perceived.
This matter is difficult to understand;
it shall be explained through analogies.
These are the fundamental body and the true mind.
It is like the moon in the sky:
it has no beginning and no end,
and it is not fully complete.
There is no arising and no passing away, no coming and no going;
sentient beings see falsely and speak of birth and extinction.
So it is with the great oceans, the rivers, and the ponds.
In streams, ponds, canals, bathing pools, and spring sources,
it universally manifests myriad reflections like the true moon;
body and mind, as well as mental states, are like the reflection of the moon.
Contemplating the body, its burning desire is very much like this;
the body’s original truth and falsehood are likewise so.
The moon in the void neither comes nor goes.
The false perceptions of ordinary beings appear amidst the various waters;
though they neither come nor go, and neither arise nor cease,
they are very much like the moon in the sky.
Although they manifest the various forms and appearances of the six realms of existence,
the body of the Tathāgatagarbha never changes.
It is like a magician who dons the skins of beasts and manifests the various images of flying birds and running animals.
The distinctions between noble and base, male and female;
the beautiful and the ugly, as well as the old and the young;
and the various laughable things in the world.
Although a magician performs various transformations,
the original form of the man never changes; likewise,
although ordinary beings undergo the forms of the six realms of existence, [the fundamental nature remains unchanged].
The color of the Tathāgatagarbha does not change;
its fundamental body and true mind are like a magician who,
while asleep, has no thoughts or perceptions, remaining tranquil and unchanging.
The body, the bodies, and the mental factors—
because they are like the playful displays of a magician— they manifest the forms of the six destinies and various laughable things.
These are the bodies and the essence of sentient beings.
This teaching through difficult-to-understand parables states that,
according to the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),
there is neither nirvāṇa nor saṃsāra.
For example, when one is in deep sleep and sees various things in a dream,
the substance of the mind is already empty and non-existent.
How much more so regarding dream-objects?
Although one clearly remembers them upon waking, in reality they do not exist;
such is the inverted consciousness of these ordinary worldlings.
The analogy is likewise:
meditative concentration and wisdom can awaken to and comprehend it,
whereas other distracted states of mind cannot understand it.
All ordinary beings are like dreams and illusions,
like the various phenomena of the moon's reflection appearing in water.
Furthermore, it is the same for all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, who are likewise holy.
From the initial generation of the bodhicitta until the attainment of the fruit of Buddhahood,
his observance of the precepts, meditative concentration, and various other activities involve a profound state of mind that remains unchanging;
yet his wisdom and supernatural powers manifest as diverse illusory transformations.
The Dharma-body is immovable;
like the moon in the sky, it universally manifests form-bodies to perform the work of a Buddha.
Although it is without coming or going, and without birth or extinction.
It is also like the reflection of the moon appearing in all waters.
Why is this? As it is said in the sūtras and śāstras:
If one wishes to study the samādhi of omniscience,
one must necessarily cultivate all wholesome states of mind;
while in samādhi, one will be able to know the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of worldly phenomena.
He also knows the supramundane noble paths of the three vehicles;
through the meditative wisdom that restrains the mind,
there is nothing he cannot accomplish.
Seeking the Buddha-way, he maintained the pure precepts and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of dhyāna and contemplation;
having attained supernormal powers, he was able to subdue the celestial Māras.
He destroys the heterodox paths,
is able to deliver sentient beings, and cuts off their afflictions.
A question is asked:
In the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras, the Buddha himself said:
"Those who wish to train as śrāvakas should train in the Prajñā[pāramitā]."
Those who wish to study the path of the pratyekabuddha should study the Prajñāpāramitā;
those who wish to study the path of the bodhisattva should study the Prajñāpāramitā.
Furthermore, there are six pāramitās,
of which Prajñā is the precursor;
it is also the mother of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Why do you now praise meditation alone, rather than praising the five pāramitās?
Furthermore, as it is said in the sūtras:
The five perfections are like the blind;
Prajñā is like the eye.
What do you think now?
You have praised deliverance while failing to praise the clear eye.
Who could believe this? We pray that you will explain it extensively and dispel our doubts.
He replied:
"Listen attentively and reflect upon it well;
I shall explain it to you with definitive certainty."
The Prajñā of the three vehicles is a single contemplation; the distinctions of realization vary according to depth.

Just as the waters of the great ocean neither increase nor decrease, yet differ according to the size of the vessels from which they are drawn— so it is with the wisdom of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the Tathāgata.
The twelve links of dependent origination are known through four kinds of wisdom: Lower wisdom belongs to the śrāvakas; middle wisdom to the pratyekabuddhas;
Subtle wisdom is called the superior wisdom of the bodhisattvas; The Tathāgata’s sudden awakening is the supreme-of-the-supreme wisdom, which transforms sentient beings through nameless dharmas.
These are distinguished by the provisional names of skillful means.
The wisdom of the three vehicles cannot know it; Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, knows it alone.
As in the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, the various Four Truths and the practices of the three vehicles share one and the same meaning.
Cunda bowed his head and addressed the World-Honored One: "The Bodhisattvas of the ten directions have gathered in this great assembly."
"What is meant by a 'Dharma-practicing bhikṣu'? We pray that the Buddha will expound the meaning of practicing the Dharma.
At that time, the Buddha told Kauṇḍinya: "Listen with a sincere and attentive mind; I shall now speak.
If there are bhikṣus who seek the practice of the Dharma, they should recite the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s scriptures."
That is to say, the Sūtras and the Abhidharma, the Upadeśas and the Vinaya—delighting in expounding these for the sake of the fourfold assembly;
yet, while delighting in reciting and preaching, they do not practice the Dharma.
Furthermore, if there are other bhikṣus who recite the twelve divisions of the Tathāgata’s scriptures...
One who can extensively expound upon and contemplate the meaning, delighting in the practice of contemplating the non-existence of phenomena;
furthermore, if there are bhikṣus who further recite the twelve divisions of the sūtras,
expounding upon and contemplating their meaning— this is called delighting in the practice of contemplating the non-existence of phenomena.
Now, the practice of the Dharma is common to the Three Vehicles. As for the one contemplation that I shall now explain:
there is a bhikṣu who is able to contemplate body and mind;
his mind does not greedily cling to any signs, he is humble and lowly-minded, and does not give rise to pride; he does not use the water of craving to irrigate the field of karma.

One does not plant the seeds of consciousness therein; with the cessation of applied and sustained thought, the sphere of objects is stilled, one is forever free from afflictions, and the mind is tranquil.
When a bhikṣu contemplates the body and mind in this way, the Buddha says that such a person truly practices the Dharma; such a bhikṣu is then able to attain [the goal].
The Bodhi of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas— A Dharma-practicing bhikṣu contemplates these three matters:
contemplating the body, contemplating feelings, and contemplating the mind.
Having observed these three mindfulnesses, the bhikṣu attains one-pointedness of mind, the four dhyānas, and the eighteen knowledges. Furthermore, it is said in the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra:

Śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all buddhas—though they equally realize the path through the four dhyānas and the eighteen knowledges (vidyās) of the two [vehicles]—differ in their clarity or obscurity.
They collectively contemplate the Four Noble Truths and the twelve links of dependent origination, yet they experience various differences according to their respective capacities for awakening.
For śrāvakas, this occurs within sixteen moments of mind regarding the Four Noble Truths.
The Pratyekabuddhas and Solitary Realizers possess untainted wisdom, and the Bodhisattvas likewise understand the teachings of the Two Vehicles and attain the sixteen truths of unimpeded knowledge.
Just as when various devas eat from a single precious vessel,
the color of their rice differs— some being black and others white— the analogy of the Four Truths is like that described in the "Lamp Chapter."
Concentration is like pure oil, and wisdom is like the wick; Dhyāna and prajñā are like the emission of great light that illuminates objects without duality—this is Prajñāpāramitā.
The lamp’s brightness is fundamentally without distinction, yet for the observer, the eyes perceive clarity or darkness differently;
So it is with dhyāna-samādhi, the factors of the path, and the six perfections.

The single dharma of prajñā is non-dual; awakening, the path, and supernormal powers all arise from dhyāna, though they manifest differently according to the capacities of those to be converted. Question:
In which sūtra does the Buddha state that prajñā and all forms of wisdom arise from meditative concentration (dhyāna)?
The answer is:
As stated in the *Dhyāna-samādhi-śāstra*,
all wisdom of the three vehicles arises from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
In the Prajñā-śāstra,
there is also this statement:
"Prajñā is born from dhyāna."
"You possess no knowledge;
you do not understand the Buddha's words and have thus given rise to doubt."
You raise such a deluded objection;
why do you not see the Buddhas of the ten directions?
When one wishes to preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings,
one first enters meditative concentration and,
by means of supernormal powers, [proceeds].
He is able to cause the great earth and the worlds of the ten directions to quake in six ways and to transform the lands in three ways.
Transforming the foul into the pure,
or even up to seven transformations,
they are able to cause all manner of unprecedented events to occur.
All these appeared in full,
delighting the hearts of the multitude and emitting great radiance.
It shines universally throughout the ten directions,
and bodhisattvas from other lands all come to assemble there.
Furthermore, one observes their dispositions and inclinations with the five eyes before teaching the Dharma.
Moreover, it is stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā-āloka-vyākhyā*:
Someone questioned the Buddha:
"The Buddha is an omniscient person whose wisdom is sovereign."
One should preach the Dharma immediately;
for what reason does one first enter meditative concentration and only thereafter preach the Dharma?
Regarding the characteristic of not knowing,
the Master of the Treatise replies:
"The Tathāgata possesses all-encompassing wisdom."
Furthermore, great radiance and great supernormal powers are all attained within meditative concentration.
The Buddha now wishes to preach the Dharma of the Great Prajñā, the Great Wisdom;
he first enters meditative concentration and manifests great supernormal powers.
They emit great radiance,
illuminating all sentient beings throughout the ten directions,
as a repayment for the grace of their meditative concentration.
Thereafter, he preached the Dharma in order to shatter the attachments of the non-Buddhists—
the six teachers of the heterodox paths.
They constantly say:
"I am such-and-such wisdom," and they always and constantly speak thus regarding all things.
It was not necessary for the Buddha to enter meditative absorption;
rather, he first entered meditative absorption in order to subdue such heterodox practitioners who held such false views.
Thereafter, he expounds the Dharma.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Sūtra on Supreme Concentration*:
"If there is another person..."
There is no need for meditative concentration;
one does not personally realize the Dharma through the body,
but rather recites and studies the twelve divisions of the scriptures with a distracted mind.
Each scroll was filled to the brim;
throughout the worlds of the ten directions, he recited them from memory with complete mastery.
Furthermore, he exerted great diligence.

To lecture upon and explain this sutra for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges is not equal to contemplating it and entering meditative concentration for even a single thought-moment.
Why is this? Because even one who has merely resolved to sit in meditation,
though they have not yet attained meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi), [is already on the path].
"He has already surpassed all the masters of debate throughout the ten directions;
how much more so those who have attained meditative concentration.
When these words were spoken,
Five hundred masters of the treatises came to where the Buddha was and,
together, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We are all of great learning."
He mastered the twelve divisions of the sutras as well as the five sections of the Vedas,
and he expounded upon the Vinaya with unimpeded eloquence.
"The sixteen great nations revere me as they do the Buddha, the World-Honored One; why,
then, do they not praise my great learning and wisdom?"
He praised meditative concentration alone.
The Buddha told the various masters of treatises,
"Your minds are distracted."
Even if one possesses great learning, what benefit is there?
You wish to compete in strength with meditative concentration,
like a blind person wishing to behold various forms.
It is like one without hands or feet wishing to embrace Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains;
like a bird with broken wings wishing to soar through the void;
or like the wing of a mosquito wishing to block the light of the sun and moon.
Just as it is impossible for people without a boat to cross the great ocean, so it is with you,
the masters of debate.
It is likewise so.
To wish to measure meditative concentration is impossible.
Furthermore, it is said in the *Vibhāṣā*:
"If there is a bhikṣu who is unwilling to practice seated meditation..."
The body does not realize the Dharma;
with a distracted mind, one reads, recites,
and expounds upon mere words and letters.
They take analytical exposition as their capability;
not knowing, they falsely claim to know;
not understanding, they falsely claim to understand.
Lacking self-awareness,
such a teacher prides himself on his own mind and treats those who practice seated meditation with contempt.
Upon death, they enter hell;
there they swallow glowing iron balls,
and upon emerging, they become flying birds.
The bodies of pigs, sheep, and other domestic animals;
chickens, dogs, jackals;
and foxes, wolves, and the like.
Furthermore, if there is a person who does not associate with virtuous friends,
even though they practice seated meditation and attain the four dhyāna concentrations.
There is no transformative cultivation;
lacking the wisdom of skillful means,
one cannot sever the afflictions.
Although one attains the bliss of tranquility and afflictions do not arise,
when one attains the four dhyānas,
one thinks that one has attained the path to nirvāṇa, which is cessation.
He then thought to himself:
"I have now attained the fruit of Arhatship;
I shall not be born again."
Such a bhikṣu has not truly attained the Way and has not severed the afflictions.
They merely attain a meditative concentration that resembles the Path,
yet they do not draw near to spiritual friends and lack the wisdom of skillful means.
That is to say, having attained what they believe to be the true path,
they give rise to overweening pride; then,
at the time of death, they see the place where they are to be reborn.
He immediately gave rise to doubt and regret, thinking:
"One who is an Arhat does not give rise to [such thoughts] again;
yet now I have given rise to them once more."
"One should know that the Buddhas have deceived me.
When he thought this,
he immediately fell into hell.
How much more so for other people who do not practice seated meditation?
To restate this meaning,
he spoke these verses:
Desiring to seek deliverance for oneself and for all sentient beings, one should universally practice the six perfections throughout the ten directions.
First, resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of bodhicitta; cultivate patience and firmly uphold the precepts;
diligently repent during the six periods of day and night; and give rise to a heart of great compassion and equanimity.
With great diligence, not sparing even body or life, Seeking the Buddha-way, they uphold the pure precepts;
Devotedly practicing meditation and wisdom, they attain supernormal powers;
Able to subdue celestial Māras and defeat non-Buddhists, They can deliver sentient beings and sever afflictions, From the first arousal of the mind until the attainment of Buddhahood.
With one body, one mind, and one wisdom, for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings,
the names and designations of the myriad practices differ; desiring to awaken to all Buddha-dharmas,
they uphold the pure precepts and cultivate meditative concentration, relinquishing all fame and gain.
Distant from the clamor and foolish retinues, Mindful of the Buddhas of the ten directions,
they constantly repent; Disregarding body and life, they seek the Buddha-way, Attaining the one hundred and eight gates of samādhi,
As well as five hundred dhāraṇīs, And various liberations and great compassion.
The five eyes, the six supernormal powers, and omniscience; Also attaining the three knowledges and the eight liberations,
Being fully endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, The thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics,
the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the six perfections, And the eighteen unique, sublime qualities.
Regarding all sentient beings as an only son, possessing the four great vows,
the four means of integration, the four immeasurable minds, and the knowledge of the paths; with the knowledge of all modes,
observing sentient beings through the four bases of miraculous power, he extensively bestows the gift of Dharma and enters the four dhyānas to radiate light.
Universally illuminating all worlds of the ten directions, Transforming filth into purity with great trembling,
Manifesting all manner of marvelous and rare events, The Bodhisattvas of the ten directions have all assembled;
The celestial kings of the three realms are all present here, Sitting upright, gazing up with single-minded devotion.
With one voice, they made three requests to hear the Dharma; He arose from the samādhi of meditative skillful means and preached the Dharma for the assembly according to their needs.

Though his physical body manifested various distinctions of fragrance and sound, His mind remained tranquil in dhyāna-concentration, unchanged; Although he sat upon his seat, he manifested the Dharma-body.

Pervading all ten directions and the nine realms of existence without exception, through the power of pure precepts, meditative concentration, and samādhi, he sees clearly and distinctly throughout the ten directions.
Those who are ready to be saved appear as if before his eyes;
those not yet ready to be saved he does not see—just as the moon’s reflection appears in all the waters of the sky.
In a dark room or a deep well, it does not appear;
Just as a master of illusions performs various transformations, those who are blind or sightless do not see them.
Likewise, the mirror of the Dharmakāya of all Buddhas is not seen by those who are blind, sightless, or heavily slumbering—beings hindered by the three obstructions.
If one lacks pure precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom, the Tathāgatagarbha body cannot be seen—
just as pure gold within a gold ore does not manifest when the necessary conditions are lacking.
Although sentient beings possess the Tathāgatagarbha, they do not perceive it if they do not cultivate ethical discipline and meditative concentration.
Possessing pure precepts, dhyāna, and wisdom, one fulfills the six perfections; thus the pure Dharma-body is manifested.
Like refined, exquisite gold mixed with mercury, it can coat various images in the world;
the Tathāgata-garbha, like gold mixed with meditative concentration, manifests through the supernatural powers of the Dharma-body to go forth and respond to beings.
I universally announce to those seeking the Way in future generations: If you do not cultivate precepts and meditative concentration, you shall be unable to attain anything by force.
Those lacking precepts, concentration, and wisdom should not engage at all;
With a hurried and distracted mind, they merely lecture on words and letters, And upon death enter hell to swallow iron pellets. When they emerge, they become animals for the duration of many kalpas.
Such sentient beings do not know themselves; They claim for themselves "I possess great wisdom," and they disparage all who sit in meditation.
They corrupt and disrupt the True Dharma, performing the works of Māra.
Even if they were to preach the sutras for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, They would never have understood the meaning of the Buddha-dharma.
To kill all the people of the three thousandfold world system, And all classes of sentient beings,
With a haughty mind slandering dhyāna and disrupting the assembly— The gravity of such a sin exceeds even this.
It is like a band of thieves plundering cow’s milk, While loudly proclaiming they have obtained the flavor of ghee.
Not knowing how to churn or heat it, one loses even the whey, the fresh butter, and the refined butter;
when even these coarse, shallow, and thin flavors are entirely lost, where can the supreme flavor of *sarpis* (clarified butter) remain?
Without practicing meditation and wisdom, there is no joy in the Dharma; as the parable says, it is like being without women.
With impure and distracted minds, they cling to mere words; thus it is said that a leather bag can be filled with anything.

Like a blind dog gnawing at a thicket of grass, seeing neither man nor non-human being, yet hearing only the sound of the wind rustling through the grass, he cries out in a loud voice, "A thief! A tiger has arrived!"
Because they nourish a blind dog that has been bitten by a tiger, the entire world’s blind dogs bark and clamor;
their minds are distracted and utterly unsettled. Their discursive thought (*vitarka*) and investigation (*vicāra*), as well as their speech, are likewise:
though they recite hundreds of thousands of sutras, their minds are constantly in turmoil, like a snake spitting venom and quarreling with the world.

you should not raise the objection that the Buddha is not impartial. For what reason?
The assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* speaks only of the single vehicle (*ekayāna*), the most sudden among the sudden, the wisdom of all Buddhas;
it is for great bodhisattvas to receive the Tathāgata’s prediction,
and it is difficult to believe and difficult to understand.
Therefore, those of the two vehicles who have exhausted their outflows,
as well as bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds and those bodhisattvas who are non-retrogressive,
are unable to resolve their doubts.
How much more so for others?
It is like the Universal Monarch (cakravartin) of the world,
who adorns the four continents.
He assembled all the wheel-turning kings to discuss the affairs of the noble king;
there was only the wise minister by the king's side.
Only then can one believe and understand,
gain proximity to the royal throne,
and participate in discussions concerning state affairs.
Other wicked ministers,
being foolish, ignorant, and lacking wisdom,
are incapable of hearing it.
They must not sit on the same seat;
how much less so other minor kings or various servants who would approach the royal throne.
The Tathāgata’s sudden teaching is also like this;
there is only the Great Being, the Immaculate One who is in his final birth before Buddhahood.
Only those who have attained the wisdom of a Buddha and received the Tathāgata’s prediction shall be able to hear it.
This assembly does not expound the teachings for those who require guidance;
therefore, others may not remain in these seats,
for if others were to hear this, they would not understand it.
They immediately give rise to doubt and slander,
falling into hell;
for this reason, they are moved and placed in another land.
The fourfold assembly of five thousand was likewise so. It was,
for example, like people of Jambudvīpa who cannot see the various devas of the higher realms with their eyes.
If one were to see it,
both eyes would become blind,
due to a lack of merit.
They were unable to behold the radiance of these devas;
therefore, those who saw it had both eyes go blind. It was likewise for the devas, asuras, and those in the three miserable realms or the eight difficulties.
They cannot even see the light of the prediction between the eyebrows received by the fleshly eye,
let alone hear the proclamation of the Tathāgata’s prediction.
If they were to hear it...
They will then give rise to slander,
forever lose their faith,
and sever all roots of goodness.
Acting as an icchantika,
he protects their feelings so that they do not hear [this teaching].
For example, it is like a person in the world who is emaciated by hunger and illness after having gone without food for a long time;
such a person with a thin stomach must not suddenly consume a large amount of dry parched grain, hard cakes, coarse flour, or strong wine.
If one were to eat a full meal at once,
death would surely follow without a doubt.
So it is for the fourfold assembly of five thousand, the devas, humans, asuras, and those in the three miserable realms and eight difficult conditions.
It is likewise so.
Because their merit is meager,
they are incapable of hearing or receiving the Tathāgata’s prophecy.
Question: The supernatural powers and immeasurable skillful means of the Buddhas enable them to preach the Dharma with a single voice,
such that beings understand it according to their respective types.
Why was it moved and placed in another land?
He replied:
"It is as you have asked."
The sounds from other lands have two meanings.
First, the native land.
Because all sentient beings cannot understand this Tathāgatagarbha,
they crave good and evil karma and transmigrate through the six realms of existence.
Second, all sentient beings have,
throughout immeasurable kalpas,
constantly remained within the six realms of existence.
Not departing from saṃsāra,
it is like one's own home;
it is also called the native land.
Because the devas, humans, asuras, and others possess meager merit,
they are unable to perceive the threefold transformation of the seats,
nor can they hear the profound and wondrous sound of the teaching on original non-arising (mūla-abhāva).
This fundamental non-existence is suchness; the suchness of the Tathāgata is one suchness, without duality. From beginning to end, it is ultimately equal.
Only Buddhas and Buddhas can know this;
other people do not understand it.
The fourfold assembly of five thousand people, devas, humans, asuras, and those in the three miserable realms or the eight difficulties,
do not hear that all things are fundamentally non-existent and like an illusion; thus,
they fail to attain ultimate liberation.
Therefore, it is called "placing [them] in other lands.
Furthermore, there were five thousand devas, humans, asuras, and those from difficult places,
each with a different seat and a different teaching.
Their understanding is meager;
they shall forever abandon the six realms of existence.
For this reason, they are further said to be "placed in other lands."
In truth, it does not move away;
one is neither aware nor conscious of it,
nor does it leave its original seat.
Because the understandings of beings differ,
it is said that there are other lands;
this is intended to restate and clarify the meaning of mindfulness of the Buddha.
And he spoke in verse:
"When the practitioner first contemplates the mindfulness of feeling, The three types of feelings are difficult to relinquish.
Painful feeling gives rise to all manner of fears, And also produces the nine afflictions and various harms."
Constantly harboring resentment, one devises expedient means; seizing an opportunity against an enemy, one cuts off their life.
Either, becoming enraged by the five pure desires, one gives rise to a heart of enmity; or, contending for fame and profit, one commits acts of hostility and harm.
Or, out of greed for one’s dwelling place and gain, one sees someone superior to oneself and desires to kill them.
Whether one suffers slander and ill repute, or at times wishes for others to be killed—these are the three kinds of suffering sensations:
internal sensation, external sensation, and internal-external sensation.
If you wish to sever all these painful sensations, you should regard your enemies as your own infants.
They are like parents and siblings, and like teachers and fellow students;
there is no birth from which they have not arisen. Throughout immeasurable kalpas, they have been my parents, and throughout vast eons, I have been born as their child; all are my own dear children.
When this contemplation is perfected, hatred is exhausted; One attains the mind of great loving-kindness and great compassion.
Enemies sigh with grief and give rise to remorseful hearts; As if seeing their own parents, they all take refuge in me.
In the past, I was once taught by them; They are all my great teachers.
Some practice worldly etiquette and the Five Classics; some study the supramundane path of liberation.
Because they study wholesome dharmas, their good reputations spread; because they endure affliction and harm, they attain supernormal powers.
All of these are my preceptors, as well as my teachers and fellow students.
One should be filial and diligently make offerings, Reverently honoring them as if they were the Buddha.
Should one enjoy the exquisite pleasures of the five senses, Or the sovereign delights of the realms of humans, devas, and kings—
The joys of the celestial kings of the three realms and of human monarchs— When impermanence arrives, all shall be shattered and destroyed.
All pleasant sensations are the root of suffering; when the retribution of pleasure is exhausted, the retribution of suffering arrives.
To greedily grasp at glory and splendor, claiming them to be permanent, leads to the arrival of hellish suffering at the time of parting from what one loves.
When pleasant sensations are exhausted, there is no more suffering; that which is neither painful nor pleasant is without rebirth.
Possessing the five expedient means, one eliminates the five desires; one also eliminates the five hindrances, which are the causes that obstruct the path.

When the afflictions of the five desires and five hindrances are exhausted, one fully possesses the five factors and enters the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.
Returning to the first dhyāna, one contemplates the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
One views the body as a bubble and emptiness as a shadow; The inhalation and exhalation are like the wind in space.

Seeing that throughout immeasurable kalpas of the past, All sensations and the five aggregates arise and perish in emptiness, One exhausts afflictions by severing the five desires, And attains the five supernormal powers by severing the five hindrances.
By severing the five desires, one attains the power of mastery; by severing the five hindrances, one attains the three types of supernormal knowledge.
Therefore, the Buddhas have spoken this verse: "Both internal and external enemies have been eliminated;
the father, ignorance, has also been extinguished and cast out. If one can sever greed, all craving will be exhausted."
Awakening oneself and awakening others is called liberation; Once the Māra-mother of all conditioned formations has been extinguished, The Māra-father of ignorance is likewise shattered.
Having severed the afflictions and attained the six supernormal powers, One establishes great vows to deliver all beings;
Having personally severed the three types of sensation, [One attains the state of non-arising.]
They also sever all sensations of sentient beings, Attaining sovereign sensations and immeasurable life;
They also know all sensations of liberation, And know the sensations of the nine destinies of ordinary and holy beings.
They also receive the prediction of a future Buddha and the prediction of a Tathāgata; If they wish to preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings,
First, he manifests rare and extraordinary wonders; entering deeply into meditative concentration, he emits radiance that universally illumines all worlds in the ten directions.

He transforms all impure and evil realms into pure lands, adorned with rows of trees made of the seven treasures, so that those in the three miserable paths and the eight difficulties are all liberated.
He brings gods and humans alike to hear the Dharma in equal measure; having observed them through the foundations of mindfulness, he then expounds the Dharma for them.

He causes the worlds—whether pure or defiled—to appear differently such that sentient beings each perceive them without knowing one another's views, their forms, colors, voices, and sounds being variously distinct.
Sentient beings each hear [the teaching] differently, And each sees the Buddha preaching the Dharma to them alone;
None perceive another before them. Though these manifestations differ and vary for each, They enable all to attain liberation simultaneously, In accordance with the length of each being’s lifespan.
One can freely experience various lifespans: Sometimes seeing a short life entering nirvana, Or seeing a long life spanning immeasurable eons.
This is the stage of the initial practice of the foundation of mindfulness of feelings;
It can sever the bonds of both suffering and pleasure. At first, one contemplates all feelings as suffering, whether internal or external.
One also contemplates that all feelings—whether internal or external—are empty; even feelings that are neither painful nor pleasant are empty.
By severing the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, one destroys ignorance. Contemplating the nature of the three types of feeling, one finds them to be neither empty nor existent;
thus, there is neither bondage nor liberation. In the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), there is no Buddha and no nirvana.
Nor is there any preaching of the Dharma to deliver sentient beings;
for sentient beings and Buddhas are of one suchness, and from beginning to end there is ultimately no distinction between them.
To sit at the site of enlightenment and attain the Buddha-way is merely the skillful means of the Teacher, like a person attaining Buddhahood within a dream.
Emitting light, he preaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings;
here there is no Buddha, no path, and no sentient beings—the nature and characteristics of the Buddha-Dharma are likewise so. Sentient beings are deluded and do not realize this;
they are deeply attached to the causes of suffering and do not abandon them even for a moment. Greed is the root of all these sufferings.
Abandoning the mind of craving and seeking, one is without dependence; Seeing that all sensations are empty and devoid of arising or ceasing, one realizes the noble truth of suffering as non-arising.
The provisional conjunction of the internal and external is called "origination";
there are no eighteen elements in the noble truth of origination. When arising and ceasing have ceased, it is called "quiescent extinction."
Realizing the noble truth of cessation, which is neither tranquil nor extinguished;
realizing the noble truth of the path, which is the wisdom of equality where the aggregates are neither bound nor liberated and there is neither wrong nor right;
these four truths are non-dual and one—this is the single truth of reality without distinction. Because this single truth is emptiness, it is the absence of any truth.
The Buddha’s three truths are skillful wisdom regarding the absence of truth;
all sentient beings, from the very beginning, are without birth or extinction, without bondage or liberation. The nature of the five aggregates is neither light nor darkness;
ordinary beings and Buddhas are not one, two, or three, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are likewise contained therein.
Because the foundation of mindfulness of feelings is predominant,
the foundation of mindfulness of feelings serves as the primary focus;
thus, by mentioning its name alone, the brief exposition of the foundation of mindfulness of feelings is concluded.
Chapter on the Foundation of Mindfulness: Furthermore,
when a practitioner first begins to practice dhyāna,
their thoughts are characterized by many discursive notions.
Applied thought and discursive investigation pursue their objects like a running monkey,
never pausing for an instant.
Even if a practitioner repeatedly observes with mental attention,
they may still be unable to collect [the mind].
He then had this thought:
"The three realms are illusory;
they are all produced by the mind."
He then contemplates from where this mind arises:
if the mind were within,
in what place would it reside?
He surveyed the interior of his body thoroughly,
but could not find the mind;
it had no place of initial birth.
Nor does it have any marks or characteristics.
If the mind were outside,
in what place would it abide?
He surveyed everything outside his body,
searching for the location of the mind,
but did not see the mind at all.
Furthermore, when observing the interval between them,
one does not perceive the mind.
When observing in this manner:
One does not perceive the mind as an internal sense base,
nor does one perceive the mind as an external sense base,
nor does one perceive the mind as both internal and external sense bases.
One does not perceive a self within the aggregates (skandhas),
nor does one perceive a self within the elements (dhātus).
One should know that this mind is empty and without a master.
It is nameless and has no course of names;
it is without characteristics and is not born from conditions.
It does not arise from non-conditions,
nor does it arise from itself;
this is what is meant by "name."
One is able to observe mental thoughts;
one observes the arising and ceasing of mental thoughts;
one observes the arising and ceasing of every moment of thought.
When observing the characteristics of each thought-moment,
because they cannot be apprehended,
there is likewise neither arising nor ceasing.
Just as one contemplates one's own mind,
so too is it with the minds of others.
Furthermore, one contemplates the nature of the mind.
There is no nature of mind;
there is no nature of mind,
nor is there any appearance.
Ultimately there is no mind,
nor is there any non-seeing of the mind.
Having observed in this way, one concludes.
With body and mind empty and tranquil,
he enters the dhyānas in succession and is able to manifest supernormal powers.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the application of mindfulness on the mind,
training to attain all meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) that arise at will.
Having established the great vow to deliver all sentient beings,
one should first contemplate their minds and enter the first dhyāna.
He enters sequentially through to the fourth dhyāna,
and so on up to the cessation of perception and feeling,
before returning to the mind of the first dhyāna.
Regarding the foundations of mindfulness: one observes the internal mind, the external mind, and both the internal and external mind;
furthermore, one contemplates the three poisons, the four great elements, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen realms, and the twelve links of dependent origination.
Having completed this contemplation,
he contemplates the samādhi of the knowledge of others' minds that pervades all liberations.
By means of the supernormal power of the knowledge of others' minds, he [proceeds].
They also enter into the universal observation of the supernormal powers of the divine eye, knowledge of past lives, and the exhaustion of outflows.
Having thus observed the seven factors of enlightenment through these supernormal powers,
they abide in the samādhi of the knowledge of others' minds.

Using the awakening factor of mindfulness, the awakening factor of discrimination of phenomena, and the awakening factor of energy, he universally contemplates the mental states, intentions, and dispositions of all sentient beings throughout the ten directions,
discerning them with the wisdom of the ten powers.
For each and every sentient being,
what Dharma do they experience upon hearing,
and what sounds do they hear?
What kind of forms and images does one see?
Through which gate of liberation does one attain liberation?
Having completed this contemplation,
by means of the samādhi of the supernatural power of the awakening factor of joy,
they cause all sentient beings of the six realms throughout the ten directions to experience great rapture.
By means of the factor of enlightenment of investigation, the factor of enlightenment of concentration, and the factor of enlightenment of equanimity,
one employs the supernormal power of the mind to universally manifest the form-body.
According to the capacities of superior, middling, and inferior roots, he taught the Dharma accordingly,
causing all to attain liberation.
When first practicing this mindfulness of mind,
one attains realization within body and mind.
He has himself severed all mental conceptions, discursive thoughts, fetters, and afflictions,
and is likewise able to teach others to train as he has done;
however, he has not yet attained supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
They lack the power of clarity;
they do not recognize that the various faculties and natures of sentient beings differ in their inclinations,
and thus they fail to accord with their capacities.
The benefit is very slight.
He reflects thus:
"This is merely the time for study."
This is not the time for such discourse;
one should not insist on speaking untimely words.
If one is practicing meditative concentration, [one should remain silent].
He attained great supernormal powers and sovereign mastery,
and achieved the samādhi of discerning the minds of others;
in a single thought-moment, he fully knew the distinctions between the minds of ordinary beings and sages.
Having mastered the past and future immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas as if they were the present age,
he thus completes his training.
Only then may one preach the Dharma.
Having completed this reflection,
he returns to the first dhyāna and contemplates his own body and mind.
Emptiness is like a shadow;
the cessation [of breath] is like the wind in space;
the mind has no form or characteristics.
Mastering lightness and emptiness,
one immediately attains supernatural powers and dwells in the fourth dhyāna.
He emits great radiance.
First, the light of form universally illumines the physical bodies of ordinary and sage beings throughout the ten directions.
Second, he emits the radiance of wisdom, which universally illumines the superior and inferior wisdom of ordinary and sage beings across the nine realms throughout the ten directions.
He is fully able to know universally what is possible and what is impossible,
as well as the causes, conditions, and karmic retributions of past lives;
this is also like the samādhis of the mindfulness of the body and the mindfulness of sensation.
In this way, he finally manifested his entire body;
throughout the ten directions, whether far or near,
it was as if facing him before one's eyes.
He preached the Dharma to each of them,
causing them all to attain liberation.
When he was about to preach the Dharma, [he...]
Manifesting rare and wondrous events,
they gladden sentient beings and cause them great joy.
By means of his supernormal powers,
he transforms the defiled and impure places of the worlds in the ten directions into pure lands.
Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and all manner of precious jewels are interspersed throughout the ground,
filling the entire world.
There were exquisite sandalwood trees made of the seven treasures,
with flowers and fruits flourishing in abundance.
The rows were symmetrical;
there were terraces, halls, watchtowers, and battlements,
as well as cities, towns, and villages.
There were chambers and couches made of the seven treasures,
and wish-fulfilling jewels whose radiance illuminated one another.
If the sun and moon appear,
it is like the pure land where the Tathāgata dwells,
filled with all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Each manifested supernatural powers,
subduing the celestial Māras and defeating all non-Buddhist heretics.
Or there may be Buddhas who,
in silent meditative concentration,
[manifest] their upper and lower limbs.
He emits great rays of light,
like masses of clouds,
which pervade the ten directions; within these rays of light, all Buddha-activities are manifested.
There may be bodhisattvas who manifest the inconceivable four great oceans of water.
Placing it within a single pore,
those belonging to the watery realm do not perceive its coming or going.
Mount Sumeru, the king of mountains, was placed within a mustard seed without being compressed;
it was then returned to its original location.
The Four Heavenly Kings and the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven neither perceive nor know that the three-thousandfold world system has been placed upon the tip of a single hair.
Nor did it lean or tilt;
the entire great assembly was not aware of any expansion or contraction,
remaining as before and no different.
Humans and devas interfaced,
both being able to see one another;
all humans and devas who had not yet attained the Way.
All the śrāvakas and bodhisattvas of minor practice were able to behold these inconceivable events,
as were the Buddhas of the ten directions and the various Caturmahārājas.
As well as the asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and so forth—
all of whom converse face-to-face with the bodhisattva;
he is able to face all their faces with a single face.
Just as the face is not different from its reflection in a mirror,
he then preaches the Dharma so that all who hear it may simultaneously attain the Way.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of the Wish-Fulfilling Power of the Mindfulness Foundation and Supernormal Powers.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and all Buddha-dharmas are entirely contained within this;
it is the fundamental basis for contemplating the mind as a station of mindfulness.
Therefore, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind is paramount.
To single out its name and proclaim the discourse on the mind,
he spoke this verse:
The internal mind, the external mind, and the intermediate mind— All these are merely mind;
the nature of mind is pure, without name or mark. It is neither within nor without, nor is it in between;
Unborn and undying, it is eternally quiescent. Neither defiled nor pure, neither bright nor dark.
Neither fixed nor distracted, neither an object of cognition; Neither moving nor staying, neither coming nor going;
Neither being nor non-being, neither death nor nirvana; Neither annihilation nor permanence, neither bondage nor liberation;
Neither the Tathāgatagarbha nor ordinary or sage— Not understanding this is called "ordinary," while understanding it is "sagehood."
When a practitioner first begins learning to seek the Way, they observe mental factors (*caitta*) and the nature of the mind (*cittatā*).
Observing mental factors is called skillful means (*upāya*); awakening to the nature of the mind is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
When first sitting in meditation, one contemplates impurity and observes the characteristics of arising and ceasing in the inhalation and exhalation of breath.
The contemplation of impurity and the mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation—these are the observation of the mind and mental factors, not the nature of the mind itself.
By observing the mind and mental factors, one severs the afflictions;

by observing the equality between the nature of the mind and the nature of the mental factors, which is itself the nature of the afflictions, one becomes fully endowed with meditative concentration and wisdom to become a Great Sage.
Through the meditation on impurity, the beginner severs the five desires; By long cultivation, one attains the supernormal power of mastery over the mind.
First, by contemplating the breath, one understands that provisional names are empty; By long cultivation, one flies through the air without obstruction.
When the two contemplations are perfected into one, One attains the three insights and perceives the three periods of time.

Mindfulness of the body, mindfulness of sensation, and mindfulness of phenomena—these three types of awareness are realized through contemplating the mind as being conventionally designated internally, externally, and both internally and externally. These three conventional designations are not substantial dharmas;
the mindfulness of the mind is neither conventional nor truly real. Having sought the realization of these three conventions, one should contemplate the mind.
The first is called the characteristic of mind; the second is called its nature. The third is provisional existence, which arises through characteristics and not through nature.
From ignorance as condition up to old age and death, all these are created by the characteristics of mind.
These include this provisional body and all sensations, as well as wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate dharmas.
All arise from the activity of the deluded mind; If one contemplates that the deluded mind has no place of origination, then there is neither affliction nor ignorance.
The nature of the mind is thoughtless and cannot be observed;
when the mental conceptions of the four foundations of mindfulness are exhausted, Afflictions are exhausted, and thus there is the knowledge of exhaustion.
If one contemplates the nature of the mind and realizes the four foundations of mindfulness, one understands the dharma of non-arising;
through the wisdom of non-arising, there is no deluded thought and no objective conceptualization. Because there is no defilement, there are no six realms of existence.
If a person follows along with deluded thoughts, yet maintains the precepts and practices seated meditation in the desire to seek the Way—

Just as rain alters the colors of dyed robes, if one does not realize the outflow-free state while clinging to the flavor of dhyāna, one will fail to attain liberation and return to the four realms of existence.
How much more so for those who break the precepts, lack meditative concentration, possess inverted and distracted minds, and cling to mere words;
the nature of the mind is pure, like a bright pearl.
It is not defiled by various colors; it is like a pure wish-fulfilling gem placed within water wrapped with objects of various hues.
It can cause the clear water to change according to those colors:
when wrapped with a blue object, the water becomes blue; yellow, red, white, and black likewise all change accordingly.
The color of the jewel is tranquil and unchanging; the nature of the mind is pure like a wish-fulfilling gem.

The colors of mixed conditions—good and evil karma—are variegated: practicing the ten wholesome paths with outflows leads to rebirth in the heavens, while committing the ten unwholesome deeds leads to birth in the four realms of existence.
By maintaining pure precepts and cultivating meditative concentration and wisdom, one attains purity.
Realizing the untainted path of liberation, from the limit of saṃsāra to nirvāṇa, the nature of mind is tranquil and immutable.
It is like a worldly wish-fulfilling gem that manifests in accordance with whatever one seeks; the gem has no mental characteristics and no discursive thoughts.
Pervading everywhere according to whatever is sought or remembered, the nature of mind is without substance and without name;

it manifests as ordinary or holy beings according to the karma of those who train. If a person desires to seek the path to liberation, they should be fully endowed with the ten wholesome actions and contemplate the three natures:
the nature of mind, the nature of the eye, and the nature of the intellect.
Fully endowed with the three faiths and the three liberations, Contemplating body and mind as empty while upholding pure precepts, one realizes True Suchness;

this is called the liberation of faith and precepts. Contemplating the body as like a shadow or a magically conjured being, Contemplating the mind as having no master and no name, And contemplating transgression and non-transgression as like dreams and illusions.
Even at the cost of one's life, one does not break the precepts; by upholding the precepts, one ultimately realizes nirvana.
Swiftly departing from the discrimination of signs, though the precepts are empty, one is neither entangled with the world nor attached to emptiness, yet follows worldly dharmas.
One deeply enters into the intention of liberation and nirvana.
Not abandoning the ten wholesome actions of the world, Attaining untainted meditative concentration and wisdom,
with a mind free from distraction and fixed in faith; Cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness, severing the four inversions,
and realizing the single characteristic of the four noble truths— This is called Prajñāpāramitā.
The nature of all phenomena is suchness; faith is likewise suchness. If a person is endowed with these three kinds of faith, that person may then obtain the gift of Dharma.
Faith, generosity, ethical discipline, learning, wisdom, shame, and remorse—these seven riches are called the guide.
If one is not endowed with these seven qualities, [one cannot lead others].

Such a person should not ascend the high seat; lacking faith and realization, they do not know for themselves what they are saying as they speak falsely to the assembly. This person deceives themselves and deceives others;
with a hurried and distracted mind, they slander the Buddha’s teaching—just like a wealthy elder who possesses his own riches.
The Dharma-giving practiced is called "giving according to reality. If a person cultivates the Path and realizes liberation, they are like a wealthy elder who practices giving according to reality.
Those who receive and those who study should all emulate this;
having first realized it for themselves, they speak according to reality as they have attained it. One should not be hasty or confused, thereby bringing disorder upon future generations.
The Buddha’s intent is profoundly deep and difficult to know; Only through practicing according to the teaching can one realize it.
Although this nature is empty and devoid of arising or ceasing, There will certainly be retribution for rejoicing in evil karma.
Just as space has neither light nor darkness, Yet light and darkness appear when wind, clouds, stillness, and turbulence occur.
If at dawn there is no wind or clouds, the sun rises and the void is brilliantly clear and pure;
yet if black clouds suddenly arise in turmoil, or if dust, mist, and great black winds appear,
the nature of the void remains stainless and pure, unstained by light or darkness.
The nature of the minds of sentient beings is likewise: Neither birth-and-death nor nirvana can defile it.
The nature of the minds of sentient beings is likewise: It is not defiled by the extremes of annihilationism or eternalism.
If the nature of the minds of sentient beings were impermanent, It would perish and disintegrate moment by moment, and there would be no karmic retribution.
If the nature of the minds of sentient beings were permanent, Like space, unchanging and devoid of karmic retribution;
And if the nature of the mind were not non-permanent— For it is through the removal of afflictions that one attains liberation from birth and death,
And because this liberation is never lost— If one says the nature of the mind is not non-permanent, [it would follow that there is no liberation].
If one seeks the Way, one should not attain liberation;
if one attains liberation by abandoning birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), one should know that liberation is impermanent.
If the nature of birth-and-death cannot be abandoned, one should know that there is no liberation. If it is said that birth-and-death cannot be abandoned...
The words of this person cannot be abandoned; if one says that birth and death can be abandoned, the words of this person cannot be relied upon.

whether it be swiftness or slowness, or what is possible and what is impossible,
each person will accordingly perceive and hear them.
Their colors, forms, sounds,
and names are each distinct and different.
All have attained the Noble Path.
Yet there may be sentient beings who cannot be transformed through teaching.
Even if one were to employ the supernatural powers of preaching the Dharma and manifesting transformations, there would be nothing that could be done [to save them].
There may be sentient beings who,
if the Dharma is preached to them first...
Even when manifesting supernatural powers,
they are unable to give rise to faith;
one must first engage in common activities and allow them full indulgence in the five desires.
Furthermore, by means of other skillful methods regarding matters concerning the breaking of precepts,
he causes the mind of desire to find rest and preaches the Dharma accordingly.
One can thus attain the Way.
Having completed such contemplation,
one demonstrates it to all sentient beings.
Only those worldly affairs that can be transcended are visible.
Others do not see it.
Thus he deliberates and observes the mind of his disciple.
And he preaches the Dharma for them;
this is called preaching the Dharma well,
so as not to cause attachment to sensory objects.
Among the ten epithets, he is named Sugata Buddha.
Observing in this manner, he enters the first dhyāna;
arising from the first dhyāna, he enters the second dhyāna.
Emerging from the second dhyāna, one enters the third dhyāna;
emerging from the third dhyāna, one enters the fourth dhyāna;
emerging from the fourth dhyāna, one enters the four formless attainments.
Entering the four formless absorptions, one enters the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling.
Arising from the attainment of the cessation of perception and feeling, one dwells in the fourth dhyāna and contemplates the four foundations of mindfulness.
Entering the samādhi of the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas and the supernormal power of *ṛddhi*,
the worlds of the ten directions shook in six ways and emitted great radiance.
Illuminating the ten directions,
all the great bodhisattvas, as well as the humans and devas of the three realms, have all come to this assembly through the power of the four foundations of mindfulness.
It enables the great assembly to each perceive worlds of differing purity and impurity,
such that they are unaware of one another’s visions,
manifesting inconceivable supernatural transformations and immeasurable varieties of wonders.
The experience of beholding the Buddha’s body is likewise so with respect to a single dharma-gate.
With immeasurable names and unequal distinctions,
they manifest immeasurable bodies.
He preached the Dharma for the multitude,
yet each person was unaware of the others;
they saw only a single Buddha.
Within a single thought-moment, the Dharma is preached all at once;
though what is seen and heard differs for each,
the attainment of the Way is non-dual.
It is but a single dharma;
this is called the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mastery over Dharmas,
because of the accomplishment of the application of mindfulness to dharmas.
The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are also included therein; however,
the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) is the primary one,
and thus it alone is given its specific name.
The General Exposition on the Foundation of Mindfulness (*Dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is concluded.
